Security evaluations for personal AI agents have largely been conducted as text conversations. That is exactly the setting where a modern agent is strongest: a forged message in a chat window is something a language model can be trained to scrutinise. The attack surface that escapes this framing is the one an agent treats as most trustworthy — the attached image, the scanned invoice, the ID photo, the screenshot of a "system notice".

Multimodal-SEA, posted to arXiv on 5 November, moves the evaluation into that surface.

## The Benchmark

The benchmark contains **608 expert-designed tasks grounded in real-world fraud cases**, spread over **14 domains** and **152 attack scenarios**, each with prepared multimodal content. Tasks span **four difficulty levels** and deliberately mix **Chinese and English social and cultural contexts**, since social engineering is a local craft as much as a technical one.

Crucially, this is not a static question-and-answer set. Agents must **inspect content, verify requests, and execute actions inside simulated applications**, and outcomes are judged from **verifiable tool execution logs** — whether the agent actually transferred the money, shared the code, or approved the request, not whether its prose looked suspicious. A companion **multimodal attack harness** gives the red team explicit control over task information, attack progression, and multimodal content construction.

## What It Found

Seven widely used multimodal models were evaluated across six dimensions, and **all of them were vulnerable**, with attack success rates spanning **7.1% to 34.5%**.

The headline number is the comparison between the text and multimodal versions of the same attacks. **Adding multimodal content raised attack success from 19.9% to 29.2%** — and it did so *even though* agents verified more proactively when images were present. The extra verification was performed, and then defeated anyway. A forged document does not need to be persuasive in the way a persuasive email is; it only needs to look like an artefact.

Two follow-up results deserve attention. **Stronger safety instructions reduced attack success without improving recognition of deceptive multimodal content** — the instruction suppresses the action, not the perception, so the model still believes the forgery. And for some models, **lower attack success came bundled with excessive refusal of legitimate requests**. That is the real trade-off of the fix: a model tuned to be suspicious of documents becomes a model that refuses to work with documents.

## Why It Matters

Agent security has been argued mostly as an output-filtering problem — check what the model is about to say and about to do. Multimodal-SEA suggests that the binding constraint is upstream of that: an agent that reads a forged artefact as genuine has nothing left for the filter to catch. Making the perception layer trustworthy, not just the action layer, is the open problem.

Paper: [arXiv:2611.08281](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08281)
